items.prompt: What is an "edge case"?
choices: An input at the extreme or unusual end of what a function accepts — empty, zero, negative, or exactly on a threshold
Any input that causes a function to run slowly
A test written by a junior engineer
A bug that has already been fixed
items.explanation: Edge cases are inputs at the boundaries or extremes of what a function handles — as opposed to "typical" inputs from the interior of a range, which is where most manual testing naturally clusters.
items.reference:
🎯 Typical input — comfortably inside a range
⚠️ Edge case — empty, zero, negative, exactly on a threshold

Why: bugs disproportionately hide at the edges precisely because typical testing avoids them.

items.prompt: Why do edge cases matter more, per input tested, than typical "interior" inputs?
choices: Because that's where an author's mental model of the code and the actual intended behavior are most likely to silently diverge
Because edge cases are always more common in production than typical inputs
Because edge cases are easier to write test code for
They don't actually matter more — every input is equally likely to reveal a bug
items.explanation: Edge cases (especially boundaries) are exactly where a subtle mistake like `<` vs. `<=` becomes visible — interior values behave identically regardless of the mistake, so they can't reveal it.
items.reference:
🎯 Typical input — comfortably inside a range
⚠️ Edge case — empty, zero, negative, exactly on a threshold

Why: bugs disproportionately hide at the edges precisely because typical testing avoids them.

items.prompt: What is a "boundary condition"?
choices: The specific point where a function's behavior is supposed to change — the single most common place an edge-case bug hides
A rule that prevents a function from ever being called
The maximum number of arguments a function can accept
A type of error message shown to users
items.explanation: A boundary condition is the exact threshold where behavior changes — a price tier cutoff, an array's first/last index, a loop's start/end — and it's the most common location for off-by-one bugs.
items.reference:
📍 Boundary — the exact point behavior changes
🐛 Common bug — off-by-one, wrong comparison operator

Why: interior values on either side of a boundary can't reveal a boundary bug — only the boundary itself (and its immediate neighbors) can.

items.prompt: In the shipping-cost scenario, where exactly does the 5kg boundary bug live?
choices: At exactly weight = 5 — the code uses `< 5` while the business rule means "5 and under"
Throughout the entire 0-5kg range
Throughout the entire 5-10kg range
It affects every weight value equally
items.explanation: The bug's entire "surface area" is the single point where the code's comparison and the business rule disagree — every other value in both ranges behaves correctly.
items.reference:
📍 Boundary — the exact point behavior changes
🐛 Common bug — off-by-one, wrong comparison operator

Why: interior values on either side of a boundary can't reveal a boundary bug — only the boundary itself (and its immediate neighbors) can.

items.prompt: What is an "equivalence class" in the context of testing?
choices: A group of inputs a function is expected to treat the same way, so testing one representative value is efficient
A category of programming language, like "object-oriented" or "functional"
A group of test files stored in the same folder
The set of all possible bugs a function could have
items.explanation: An equivalence class groups inputs expected to produce the same kind of behavior (e.g. all weights strictly between 0 and 5kg) — testing one value from the class is efficient, as long as the class boundaries are identified correctly.
items.reference:
📦 Equivalence class — inputs expected to behave the same
✅ Efficient — test one representative, not every value

Why: this is what makes testing tractable at all — you can't test every possible input, but you can test every distinct class of behavior.

items.prompt: Why is testing one value per equivalence class only safe "if the classes and their boundaries are identified correctly"?
choices: Because if the boundary is misidentified, the interior test value could miss exactly the input where behavior actually diverges
Because equivalence classes always contain exactly one value
Because equivalence classes never actually exist in real code
Because testing interior values is always faster than testing boundaries
items.explanation: The whole approach depends on correctly identifying where one class ends and another begins — an interior test value from a correctly-identified class tells you nothing about whether the class's actual boundary matches your assumption.
items.reference:
📦 Equivalence class — inputs expected to behave the same
✅ Efficient — test one representative, not every value

Why: this is what makes testing tractable at all — you can't test every possible input, but you can test every distinct class of behavior.

items.prompt: What is an "invariant"?
choices: A property that should hold true across every valid input, not just specific examples
A value that never changes throughout a program's execution
A synonym for "edge case"
A type of syntax error
items.explanation: An invariant is a property expected to hold across the entire input space (e.g. "shipping cost never decreases as weight increases") — useful for catching bugs example tests happen to miss, though not every bug violates a stated invariant.
items.reference:
🔁 Invariant — true across every input, not just examples
⚠️ Limit — only catches bugs that actually violate it

Why: invariants generalize testing power across a whole range, but they're not a universal bug detector.

items.prompt: Is it true that if an invariant holds across every tested input, the function is definitely bug-free?
choices: No — the invariant only rules out the specific class of bug it's actually sensitive to, not every possible bug
Yes — a passing invariant check always proves complete correctness
No — invariants can never be tested, only assumed
Yes, but only for functions with fewer than three inputs
items.explanation: An invariant holding increases confidence, but it only detects violations of that specific property — a bug that doesn't happen to violate the stated invariant will pass right through, undetected.
items.reference:
🔁 Invariant — true across every input, not just examples
⚠️ Limit — only catches bugs that actually violate it

Why: invariants generalize testing power across a whole range, but they're not a universal bug detector.

items.prompt: What is an "off-by-one error"?
choices: A boundary condition using the wrong comparison (`<` instead of `<=`, or an index shifted by one), correct everywhere except exactly at the boundary
Any bug that causes a function to return the wrong data type
A bug that only happens on the first run of a program
A network error that retries exactly once too many times
items.explanation: An off-by-one error is specifically a boundary comparison mistake — the function is correct everywhere except at the exact point where the wrong comparison operator diverges from the intended one.
items.reference:
❌ < instead of <= — wrong at exactly one point
✅ Everywhere else — behaves identically either way

Why: this is precisely why interior testing can't catch it — the wrong and right comparison only disagree at one input.

items.prompt: Why can't testing a value comfortably inside a range ever reveal a `<` vs. `<=` off-by-one bug at that range's boundary?
choices: Because `<` and `<=` produce identical results for any value that isn't exactly the boundary itself
Because interior values are always invalid inputs
Because off-by-one bugs only occur in loops, never in comparisons
Because testing interior values always throws an error
items.explanation: For any value other than the exact boundary, `weight < 5` and `weight <= 5` evaluate identically — the two comparisons only diverge exactly at 5, so nothing short of testing 5 itself can distinguish them.
items.reference:
❌ < instead of <= — wrong at exactly one point
✅ Everywhere else — behaves identically either way

Why: this is precisely why interior testing can't catch it — the wrong and right comparison only disagree at one input.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why did all three of the developer's tests pass despite a real bug shipping?
choices: Each test value was chosen from comfortably inside a pricing tier, nowhere near the exact boundary where the bug lives
The developer never actually ran the tests
The bug only affects negative weight values
The tests were written after the bug was already found and fixed
items.explanation: 2kg, 6kg, and 15kg are all comfortably inside their respective tiers — none of them is anywhere near the exact 5.0 boundary where the code's `<` and the business rule's "and under" disagree.
items.reference:
🧪 Tests — 2kg, 6kg, 15kg (all interior)
💸 Real bug — exactly 5.0kg overcharged

Why: "all tests passed" and "the code is correct" are different claims — this scenario is the gap between them made concrete.

items.prompt: What specifically caused the customer's exactly-5.0kg package to be overcharged?

The customer's package was mislabeled by the shipping carrier
The developer intentionally overcharged exact-boundary weights
items.explanation: At weight = 5, `weight < 5` is false, so control falls through to the 5-10kg tier — exactly the mismatch between the code's strict-less-than and the business rule's inclusive "and under."
items.reference:
🧪 Tests — 2kg, 6kg, 15kg (all interior)
💸 Real bug — exactly 5.0kg overcharged

Why: "all tests passed" and "the code is correct" are different claims — this scenario is the gap between them made concrete.

items.prompt: L2's flowchart lists four steps for finding edge cases systematically. What comes right after "partition into equivalence classes"?
choices: Identify the boundary between each class
Write more interior test values
Delete the function and rewrite it from scratch
Ship the code to production immediately
items.explanation: After partitioning the input space into classes (under 5, 5-10, over 10), the next step is identifying the exact boundary between each class — the point most likely to hide an off-by-one bug.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Identify input space
2️⃣ Partition into classes
3️⃣ Identify boundaries
4️⃣ Test boundary ± one step, plus out-of-domain values

Why: this ordered process is what replaces "pick a few values and hope" with something systematic.

items.prompt: Why does L2's flowchart test the boundary value AND one step on each side, rather than just the boundary value alone?
choices: Because a boundary bug can go either direction — testing all three values is what distinguishes a `<` bug from a `<=` bug from correct code
Because testing only the boundary value is technically impossible in most languages
Because three tests always run faster than one test
Because the boundary value itself is never actually a valid input
items.explanation: Testing just the boundary alone can pass by coincidence — comparing behavior at the boundary against behavior on both immediate sides is what actually reveals whether a `<`/`<=` mistake exists.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Identify input space
2️⃣ Partition into classes
3️⃣ Identify boundaries
4️⃣ Test boundary ± one step, plus out-of-domain values

Why: this ordered process is what replaces "pick a few values and hope" with something systematic.

items.prompt: L2's edge-case category table lists "just past boundary" (e.g. weight = 5.01) as its own category, separate from the exact boundary. Why is it listed separately?
choices: Because it's often skipped for a different reason than the boundary itself — it feels redundant with the boundary test, even though it tests different logic
Because "just past boundary" values are always invalid inputs
Because 5.01 and 5.0 always produce identical output in every function
Because only integer values can be boundary values
items.explanation: Testing the boundary value alone doesn't confirm the OTHER side of the comparison is also correct — "just past" is its own check, skipped for its own reason (feeling redundant), not because it's less important.
items.reference:

Zero is never actually a valid input to any function
Testing zero always causes the program to crash

items.explanation: Zero often gets skipped simply because it feels like an uninteresting, trivial case to write a test for — but it's a distinct equivalence-class boundary (often the very first one) capable of hiding real bugs.

items.explanation: The bug misclassifies weight = 5 into the more expensive tier — the price still goes up, not down, as weight increases, so "never decreases" remains true even at the buggy input.
items.reference:
✅ Invariant holds — price never decreases, bug and all
❌ Still wrong — price at exactly 5.0 is the wrong tier

Why: this is the central lesson of L2 — a real, meaningful invariant can hold true right through a real, shipped bug.

items.prompt: What's the core lesson L2 draws from monotonicity holding despite the shipping-tier bug?
choices: A specific invariant only catches the specific class of bug it's actually sensitive to — it isn't a substitute for directly testing likely boundaries
Invariants are never useful and should not be checked
Monotonicity is the wrong invariant to ever check for pricing functions
The bug doesn't actually exist since the invariant passed
items.explanation: The lesson isn't "don't use invariants" — it's that an invariant's power is bounded by what it actually checks; boundary-value testing catches a class of bug invariants like this one structurally can't.
items.reference:

❌ Still wrong — price at exactly 5.0 is the wrong tier

Why: this is the central lesson of L2 — a real, meaningful invariant can hold true right through a real, shipped bug.

items.prompt: L2 argues that writing ten more interior test values (2.1kg, 3.7kg, 8.2kg...) would still miss the 5.0kg bug. Why?
choices: Because more interior values are still the same KIND of test — none of them is the exact boundary value where the bug actually lives
Because JavaScript limits functions to at most six test cases
Because interior values become less reliable the more of them you add
Because the bug only appears on the tenth test run, not before
items.explanation: Adding more interior samples doesn't change what kind of input is being tested — the bug's entire surface area is one specific point, and no number of interior samples gets closer to hitting it.
items.reference:
🔁 More of the same — more interior values, same blind spot
🎯 Different kind of test — the boundary itself, deliberately targeted

Why: "more tests" only helps if the new tests are actually a different category, not just more of the same category.

items.prompt: According to L2, what's the actual fix for the "one value per case isn't enough" problem — is it "test more values"?
choices: No — the fix is reasoning about the structure of the input space (boundaries, equivalence classes) rather than adding more of the same kind of sample
Yes — the only fix is to test every possible numeric value
No — the fix is to remove all boundary conditions from the code
Yes — doubling the number of tests always finds all bugs
items.explanation: The fix is a different process, not a bigger version of the same process — systematically identifying boundaries and equivalence classes finds the specific inputs worth testing, rather than hoping quantity alone gets there.
items.reference:
🔁 More of the same — more interior values, same blind spot
🎯 Different kind of test — the boundary itself, deliberately targeted

Why: "more tests" only helps if the new tests are actually a different category, not just more of the same category.

items.prompt: Implement `checkMonotonic(fn, maxInput, step)`. Starting from `fn(0)`, step through inputs from `step` to `maxInput` in increments of `step`, calling `fn` at each. If any value is less than the previous value, return `{ violated: true, at: <input>, prev: <previous value>, cur: <current value> }`. If the loop completes without any decrease, return `{ violated: false }`.

tests.description: a genuinely non-decreasing function reports no violation
tests.expr: (() => { const fn = (x) => Math.floor(x / 5); const r = checkMonotonic(fn, 20, 1); return expect(r.violated).toBe(false); })()

tests.description: a function that decreases at some point is caught, with the correct 'at' value
tests.expr: (() => { const fn = (x) => (x === 10 ? 0 : x); const r = checkMonotonic(fn, 20, 1); expect(r.violated).toBe(true); return expect(r.at).toBe(10); })()

tests.description: the shipping tier bug does NOT get caught by this invariant (monotonicity still holds)
tests.expr: (() => { function shippingCostBuggy(w) { if (w < 0) throw new Error('neg'); if (w < 5) return 4.99; if (w < 10) return 8.99; return 14.99; } const r = checkMonotonic(shippingCostBuggy, 20, 0.5); return expect(r.violated).toBe(false); })()

tests.description: prev and cur are reported correctly when a violation is found
tests.expr: (() => { const fn = (x) => (x === 3 ? 1 : x); const r = checkMonotonic(fn, 5, 1); expect(r.prev).toBe(2); return expect(r.cur).toBe(1); })()

items.explanation: Walking through the input range and comparing each output to the previous one directly checks the monotonicity invariant. This is L3's exact checkMonotonic — node-verified to correctly flag a genuine decrease, and, just as importantly, verified NOT to flag the shipping-tier boundary bug, since that bug still produces a higher (not lower) price at the miscategorized input.
items.reference:
🔁 checkMonotonic — walks the range, compares each step to the last
⚠️ Limitation — the shipping-tier bug passes this check silently

Why: this is the exact function L3 uses to prove an invariant can hold true right through a real bug — a working invariant checker, and a demonstration of its limits, in one.

items.prompt: L3's failure-mode table warns against choosing "realistic" test data instead of deliberately picking boundary and extreme values. Why is realistic data actually a poor source of edge-case tests?

🎯 Boundary/extreme data — deliberately chosen, not sampled

Why: this is why deliberate boundary selection has to be a separate, explicit step — it won't happen by accident from "realistic" sampling.
